abstract:
BACKGROUND: Genomic cardiology is an emerging field integrating genetic, molecular, imaging, and digital health data to improve cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. The genetic architecture of CVD encompasses rare, high-impact variants as well as polygenic susceptibility, both of which influence disease risk, severity, and clinical outcomes.
HYPOTHESIS: Integration of genomic information, including rare variants and polygenic risk scores (PRS), with clinical, imaging, biomarker, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches may enhance personalized cardiovascular risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making.
METHODS: This review summarizes current applications and emerging developments in genomic cardiology, including whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing, multigene panels, structural variant detection, PRS, multi-omics integration, and AI-assisted risk prediction. Current challenges and emerging therapeutic approaches, including RNA-based therapies and gene editing, are also discussed.
RESULTS: Clinical genomic tools are increasingly being incorporated into the evaluation of inherited cardiac conditions. PRS can identify individuals with elevated lifelong CVD risk, although their current clinical utility is primarily as risk-enhancing markers rather than standalone diagnostic tests. Integration of genomic, clinical, imaging, and biomarker data using AI may further improve risk prediction and personalized treatment selection. However, ancestry bias, uncertainty in variant interpretation, limited accessibility, workflow integration barriers, and ethical and privacy concerns remain important challenges.
CONCLUSIONS: Genomic cardiology has substantial potential to advance precision cardiovascular medicine. Continued development of diverse genomic databases, standardized clinical implementation frameworks, and emerging genomic therapies will be important for translating genomic advances into equitable and clinically meaningful cardiovascular care.

title: From Genomics to Precision Cardiology: A Comprehensive Review of Clinical Applications and Challenges in Cardiovascular Diseases.

abstract: Ehrlich carcinoma (EC) and its ascitic form, Ehrlich ascites carcinoma (EAC), are among the oldest and most widely used experimental tumor models in cancer research. Although they have traditionally been used for anticancer drug screening, their potential to address broader aspects of aggressive tumor biology has received comparatively less attention. EC/EAC exhibits several characteristics associated with advanced malignancy, including rapid tumor growth, angiogenesis, immune dysregulation, metabolic changes, therapeutic resistance, and complex interactions between the tumor and host. These features make EC/EAC a useful complementary model for studying different aspects of tumor progression. However, research using these models has largely focused on transcriptional changes and individual signalling pathways, while post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms remain less explored. In particular, the role of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), a major component of microRNA-mediated gene regulation, is still poorly understood in EC/EAC. In this review, we discuss the major limitations of current EC/EAC research, including the limited use of multi-omics approaches, single-cell and spatial analyses, functional genomics, immune checkpoint profiling, and integrated systems-level studies. We further discuss how incorporating RISC-centered regulatory networks with emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based studies, spatial transcriptomics, and metabolic profiling could provide deeper mechanistic insights and improve the translational value of these models. Bringing together the strengths of this established tumor model with contemporary approaches in cancer biology could help reposition EC/EAC as a relevant and versatile platform for studying tumor progression and therapeutic responses.

title: Revisiting Ehrlich carcinoma in the era of precision oncology: bridging classical models with modern systems biology.

abstract: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a promising targeted radiotherapy for osteosarcoma, offering selective tumor cytotoxicity and localized energy deposition, but its efficacy is limited by heterogeneous intratumoral boron distribution. Using a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in U2OS osteosarcoma cells, we identified genetic regulators of boron uptake. GCLC deficiency markedly enhanced internalization of boron-containing agents. Mechanistically, GCLC loss depleted glutathione, triggered oxidative stress, and potentiated macropinocytosis, thereby boosting boron compound uptake. This effect was preferentially observed in tumor cells, as GCLC deficiency profoundly enhanced the uptake of boron delivery agents in tumor cells (such as U2OS and MDA-MB-231), far exceeding its impact on normal osteoblasts (HOB-SV40). In U2OS xenografts, GCLC silencing significantly enhanced preferential boron accumulation in tumors without altering normal tissue biodistribution. Our findings nominate GCLC as a druggable target to overcome boron delivery barriers in BNCT, providing a translatable strategy to improve efficacy for osteosarcoma, especially refractory cases.

title: GCLC Deficiency Enhances Cellular Uptake of BNCT Agents via Oxidative Stress-Induced Macropinocytosis.

abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a leading cause of mortality in critically ill patients with bloodstream infections (BSIs). Timely diagnosis and early initiation of guideline-concordant antimicrobial therapy are independently associated with improved survival and reduced complication rates in patients with MRSA BSIs. However, current blood culture-based detection of MRSA requires 3-7 days for definitive identification and antimicrobial susceptibility reporting, entails numerous manual steps, and frequently delays the transition from empirical to pathogen-directed therapy, thereby affecting treatment outcomes and patient prognosis. Here, we present a highly sensitive and specific CRISPR-based diagnostic platform that shortens the MRSA detection time from >70 h to ∼2 h-enabling true "sample-to-result" testing directly from whole blood at the point of care. This study develops a one-step RPA-CRISPR assay targeting the S. aureus nucA and mecA genes, with 10 copies/reaction sensitivity and no cross-reactivity. By integrating vancomycin-conjugated magnetic nanoparticles, a herringbone microfluidic chip, and a miniaturized wireless analyzer, the platform performs on-chip S. aureus capture, lysis-mediated DNA release, and dual-gene detection directly from whole blood. In a prospective, multicenter clinical evaluation of 350 hospitalized patients with suspected bacteremia, the HELP platform identified all 20 S. aureus-positive cases (including 8 MRSA-positive cases), demonstrating 100% positive percent agreement with blood culture. By delivering definitive MRSA identification in under 2 h, HELP markedly accelerates clinical decision-making, facilitates the timely initiation of targeted antimicrobial therapy, and holds strong potential for scalable deployment in primary care and resource-constrained settings.

title: CRISPR-Based Diagnostic Assay for Point-of-Care Detection of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus in patients with Bloodstream Infections.

abstract:
PURPOSE: Pemetrexed, a standard antifolate chemotherapy for non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), is often limited by acquired resistance. We investigated whether SRC kinase mediates pemetrexed resistance and whether SRC inhibition can suppress survival signaling in pemetrexed-resistant NSCLC cells.
METHODS: Pemetrexed-resistant cell lines (PC9 R, NCI-H460 R, and NCI-H3122 R) were generated through chronic pemetrexed exposure. Protein phosphorylation profiling and Western blotting identified key signaling alterations. SRC was abrogated using transient and doxycycline-inducible CRISPR/Cas9 systems, and reciprocal siRNA knockdown of SRC and thymidylate synthase (TS) was performed. Three SRC inhibitors-dasatinib, bosutinib, and saracatinib-were assessed using cell viability, colony formation, apoptosis, and cell cycle assays.
RESULTS: All pemetrexed-resistant cell lines demonstrated elevated phosphorylated SRC (p-SRC Y416) and enhanced downstream signaling. SRC knockout reduced p-SRC Y416, p-STAT3, and p-FAK, while increasing markers of DNA damage (γ-H2AX) and apoptosis (cleaved caspase-3), impairing cell viability and clonogenicity. SRC knockdown reduced TS expression in two resistant models, whereas TS knockdown did not suppress p-SRC Y416. Among SRC inhibitors, dasatinib showed the most potent, dose-dependent suppression of SRC signaling. Dasatinib also induced G0/G1 arrest, DNA damage, and apoptosis, thereby reducing colony formation.
CONCLUSION: SRC activation is a critical mechanism of acquired pemetrexed resistance in NSCLC and may contribute to resistance through TS-associated survival signaling. SRC inhibition, particularly with dasatinib, disrupts pro-survival pathways and promotes DNA damage-mediated cell death in pemetrexed-resistant cells. These findings support further investigation of SRC inhibitors, alone or with pemetrexed, as a biomarker-guided therapeutic strategy for SRC-activated pemetrexed-resistant NSCLC.

title: SRC Activation Drives Acquired Pemetrexed Resistance in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer and Is Targetable by Dasatinib.

abstract: T cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising adoptive cellular therapy for solid tumors by enabling recognition of intracellular antigens presented via human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules. Unlike chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy, TCR-T cell therapy targets a broader antigen repertoire, including cancer-testis antigens, neoantigens, and viral antigens. Recent clinical advances, highlighted by the approval of afamitresgene autoleucel in synovial sarcoma, demonstrate meaningful antitumor activity. However, several limitations remain, including HLA restriction, antigen heterogeneity, toxicity related to on-target/off-tumor effects, and mechanisms of resistance such as antigen loss and T cell exhaustion. Advances in antigen selection, gene editing, and synthetic biology are improving both safety and efficacy. Combination strategies and next-generation engineered constructs are expected to overcome current barriers. This review summarizes the biological rationale, clinical evidence, safety considerations, and resistance mechanisms of TCR-T cell therapy in solid tumors and discusses future directions to optimize their therapeutic potential.

title: T Cell Receptor-Engineered T Cell Therapy in Solid Tumors: Where We Stand and What's to Come.

abstract: Rare disease is a condition that affects a small fraction of the population. In most cases, it has a known genetic cause but could also be associated with other contributing factors. As the affected individuals may exhibit diverse symptoms due to the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, non- or misdiagnosis of rare diseases is common. Their low incidence and prevalence present an obstacle to developing new therapies despite a major unmet need with only a few treatment options available. This is particularly relevant to rare neurological disorders as there are major difficulties in studying the mechanisms of initiation and progression of the central nervous system (CNS) disorders. Recent advances in biotechnology, specifically the use of human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for modeling diseases, have been instrumental in providing a flexible platform that not only reflects the effects of genetic disturbances on the development of CNS disorders but also is capable of providing insights into complex multifactorial disorders. Whether the human iPSCs are harvested from the affected individuals or using the gene-editing tools on cells from healthy individuals, valuable models can now be made available for studying these orphan conditions. In this narrative review, we explore the benefits of using human iPSC models over the existing platforms of other primary cell lines and animal models for the disease modeling and drug discovery and discuss the limitations and future aspects of the iPSC use in the investigation of rare neurological disorders.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) are a first-line treatment for patients with epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), but the development of resistance limits long-term therapeutic efficacy. Tumor acidosis is a hallmark of the tumor microenvironment (TME) that has been shown to promote resistance to cancer therapies, suggesting that it may affect PARPi responses. In this study, we demonstrated that the acidic TME drives a p300-dependent mechanism of PARPi resistance in EOC. Pathologically acidic pH enhanced DNA damage repair, reduced PARPi-induced PARP1 trapping, and attenuated the antitumor efficacy of PARPis. A CRISPR-Cas9 screen identified p300 as a druggable mediator of acidosis-induced PARPi resistance. Mechanistically, acidic pH activated an ERK-p300-PARP1 signaling axis that acetylated PARP1 at lysine 505 (PARP1 K505Ac), thereby alleviating PARPi-mediated PARP1 trapping and DNA damage. Elevated PARP1 K505Ac was associated with clinical resistance to PARPis and poor overall survival. In patient-derived and syngeneic EOC models, pharmacologic inhibition of p300 synergized with PARPis to suppress tumor growth. Together, these findings identify p300 as a key mediator of acidosis-induced PARPi resistance and a promising therapeutic target to enhance PARPi efficacy.
SIGNIFICANCE: Tumor acidosis drives PARP inhibitor resistance by promoting p300-dependent acetylation of PARP1, which can be effectively targeted in preclinical models to reverse resistance and improve the therapeutic efficacy of PARP inhibitors.

title: Targeting p300 Reverses Acidic Microenvironment-Induced PARP Inhibitor Resistance.

abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to test the use of milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) in children with severe acute malnutrition in Sierra Leone. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Will the inclusion of MFGM in RUTF for 6-59-month-old Sierra Leonean children with severe acute malnutrition improve their neurodevelopment?
* Will the inclusion of MFGM in RUTF for 6-59-month-old Sierra Leonean children with severe acute malnutrition reduce its worst consequences: death, hospitalization, and remaining severely malnourished despite treatment?

Researchers will compare the MFGM-containing RUTF to standard RUTF, which contains skim milk powder.

Participants will:

* undergo measurement of length, weight, mid-upper arm circumference, and nutritional edema assessment every two weeks during severe malnutrition treatment
* be treated with either MFGM-RUTF or standard RUTF at a dose of 2 sachets per day for up to 12 weeks
* undergo neurodevelopmental testing using the Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool at the end of SAM treatment and 6 months later
* a subset of participants will undergo blood spot collection and stool sample collection

description:
Globally, approximately 15 million children are suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) at any one time, a number that has not declined in recent decades despite significant technological advancements in agriculture and food science. SAM is a condition of total-body depletion of the nutrients required for health and development; without treatment, 50% of affected children will die. Whereas historically children with SAM were admitted to and treated within hospitals, the advent of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) and community-based management of acute malnutrition revolutionized SAM care by allowing it to occur safely and successfully by the child's caregiver in their own home.

RUTF was designed to provide the nutrients required for physical recovery in a safe, palatable format. It is equal parts peanut paste, sugar, vegetable oil, and skim milk powder, with added micronutrients and emulsifier. At inception, attention was not specifically paid to how RUTF's composition might impact neurodevelopmental recovery in children with SAM. Research over the past decade has revealed that even following successful treatment with RUTF, children diagnosed with SAM still score 1-3 standard deviations below age-based expectations on neurodevelopmental tests. This suggests that the nutrient profile of standard RUTF is not sufficient to recover the developmental damage incurred by SAM.

Recently, progress has been made toward improving the developmental trajectory of children with SAM by altering RUTF. A randomized, blinded trial in Malawi including 2,500 children with SAM showed that improving the polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) profile of RUTF by reducing linoleic acid and adding docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) yields superior neurodevelopment 6 months after treatment, by 0.19 standard deviations on a standardized, culturally adapted neurodevelopmental test. This demonstrates that neurodevelopmental recovery in SAM is sensitive to the lipid profile of RUTF. Despite the benefits of improved PUFA RUTF, however, children with SAM remained 1 standard deviation below expectations in neurodevelopment.

The milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in mammalian milk contains a host of nutrients and bioactive compounds supportive of physical health and brain development. Bovine MFGM added to infant formula has been tested in several clinical trials and has demonstrated a reduction in infectious episodes, such as diarrhea and ear infections, as well as improvement in cognitive development, compared with infant formula not containing MFGM. In these trials and others, MFGM has been shown to be safe and well-tolerated. Currently, RUTF contains skim milk powder as its high-quality protein source, and peanut and vegetable oils as the primary sources of fat. These vegetable fat sources are deficient in the lipids provided by MFGM: sphingolipids, cholesterol, and other phospholipids such as phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, all of which play roles in brain development. It is possible that the lipids contained in MFGM may further support neurodevelopmental recovery in SAM children.

By acting as a natural emulsifier, MFGM also offers a food formulation advantage that is relevant to children with SAM. Animal model studies have demonstrated that emulsifiers can compromise the gut barrier. Children with SAM have damaged small intestinal barrier function, which can lead to translocation of gut bacteria and resulting systemic infection. As RUTF will compose nearly 100% of a child's intake for the duration of treatment - up to 3 months - it is possible that inclusion of emulsifier may impede gut healing and recovery. Considering this concern, the Manary lab ran a clinical trial in 2018-2019 testing a novel formulation of RUTF designed with oat in place of some skim milk powder and peanut, and without hydrogenated vegetable oil (standard emulsifier), because oat acts as a natural emulsifier. In this trial, children with SAM receiving the oat-RUTF had 10% absolute higher recovery and a 33% relative reduction in the worst SAM outcomes (death, hospitalization, or remaining severely malnourished). Like oat, MFGM in RUTF allows for omission of emulsifier and may yield similar benefits.

Given (1) the repeated finding that adding MFGM to infant formulas improves neurodevelopment, (2) the impaired neurodevelopment of children with SAM, (3) the current RUTF formulation lacking neuro-supportive fats provided by MFGM, (4) MFGM's natural activity as an emulsifier, and (5), the reality that RUTF provides the sole source of nutrition for children with SAM, it is plausible that adding this high-quality source of lipids and protein to RUTF may also benefit children with SAM in both immediate and long-term physical and cognitive recovery.

This will be an individually randomized, investigator/outcomes assessors-blinded, controlled clinical trial designed to determine if treatment of severely malnourished Sierra Leonean children 6-59-months of age with an RUTF made with MFGM-containing whey protein/fat concentrate will (1) improve neurodevelopment and (2) reduce a composite of poor SAM outcomes (death, hospitalization, remaining severely malnourished), compared with standard RUTF (S-RUTF). This trial will be conducted at 20 rural sites in Sierra Leone. 1600 children will be randomized 1:1 to receive 2 sachets per day of either MFGM-RUTF or S-RUTF. Children will receive their allocated RUTF and return to clinic fortnightly for repeat anthropometric measurements, illness questions, and to receive more RUTF until they achieve a clinical outcome or for a maximum of 12 weeks, at which point they will undergo Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool (MDAT) testing. Participants will be asked to return to clinic 6 (5-7) months later for MDAT testing, the global z-score from which will be the trial's co-primary outcome. A subset of participants will undergo blood spot and/or stool sample collection at the end of SAM treatment.

abstract: Mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) are frequently observed in several aggressive malignancies, including gliomas, chondrosarcomas, and acute myeloid leukemia. Mutant IDH enzymes exhibit neomorphic activity that produces the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG), leading to widespread DNA and histone hypermethylation. This aberrant epigenetic state remodels chromatin accessibility, thereby compromising both DNA repair and replication. However, the mechanisms underlying IDH mutation-induced DNA replication stress and the therapeutic potential of this vulnerability remain elusive. Through a whole-genome CRISPR screen, we defined differential genetic dependencies between IDH1 wild-type and mutant cells. We identified the G2/M checkpoint kinase PKMYT1 as a selective survival factor for IDH1-mutated cells. Pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of PKMYT1 profoundly suppresses the growth of IDH1-mutated tumor cells in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, IDH1-mutated cancer cells exhibit profound replication stress, characterized by reduced nucleotide incorporation, slowed replication fork progression, and delayed S-phase entry. D-2-HG elevates H3K9 trimethylation by inhibiting KDM4A, thereby impeding DNA replication initiation and fork progression. PKMYT1 blockade alters cell cycle timing, forcing unscheduled mitotic entry with incompletely replicated genomes, resulting in elevated DNA damage and mitotic catastrophe. Collectively, our findings demonstrate a mechanistic link between IDH1-driven epigenetic dysregulation, replication stress, and heightened reliance on the G2/M checkpoint. Our findings propose PKMYT1 inhibition as a therapeutic strategy that exploits the intrinsic replication deficiency of IDH1-mutant glioma.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen identifies PKMYT1 inhibition as a synthetic lethal vulnerability in IDH1-mutant glioma.

abstract: Buffaloes are important contributors to agricultural production in many developing countries, yet poor semen cryosurvival remains a major challenge for efficient artificial insemination and genetic improvement. In recent years, small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication and reproductive function; however, their potential as supplements for improving buffalo semen cryosurvival remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study evaluated the influence of adding a seminal plasma-derived small extracellular vesicle-enriched preparation to a Tris extender using post-thaw sperm traits, oxidative status, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and fertility of Kundhi buffalo bull semen. Seminal plasma-derived particles were isolated and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, showing a mean diameter of 117.8 ± 2.47 nm, modal diameter of 89.4 ± 1.41 nm, and concentration of (3.21 ± 0.05) × 1011 particles/mL. Thirty-two ejaculates from four Kundhi buffalo bulls were pooled and extended with a Tris extender supplemented with 0, 25, 50, 100, or 200 μg/mL sEV-enriched preparation before cryopreservation. Post-thaw sperm quality, early apoptosis, DNA fragmentation, lipid peroxidation, antioxidant enzymes, and relative mRNA abundance of HSP70 and PRM1 were assessed. All evaluated post-thaw variables differed (P < 0.05) after supplementation, whereas 50 μg/mL revealed the strongest response. The EV-50 group showed higher total motility, progressive motility, viability, and HOST-positive spermatozoa, however reduced early apoptotic sperm, DNA fragmentation, and MDA concentration than the control group. EV-50 also enhanced SOD, catalase, total glutathione, HSP70 and PRM1 expression (1.91 ± 0.07-fold and 1.69 ± 0.05-fold, respectively). In fertility validation, pregnancy rate increased from 41.7% in the control group to 56.7% in the EV-50-treated semen group, with higher odds of pregnancy (OR = 1.83; P = 0.028). In conclusion, supplementation with 50 μg/mL of the sEV-enriched preparation improved post-thaw sperm quality, redox homeostasis, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and field fertility, supporting its potential as a cryopreservation supplement for enhancing the reproductive performance of Kundhi buffalo semen.

abstract:
METHODS: Using established TLE4-overexpression and CRISPR-Cas9-knockout cervical cancer cell lines and nude mouse tumorigenesis models, we verified the biological function and regulatory mechanism of TLE4 in cervical cancer.
RESULTS: Quercetin treatment upregulated the expression of TLE4 in HeLa cells. Compared with normal cervical tissues from clinical specimens, the expression of TLE4 in the nucleus of cervical cancer tissues was significantly downregulated. Transwell assays showed that the migration and invasion of C-33A TLE4-overexpression cells were significantly suppressed, accompanied by an upregulation of the expression of E-cadherin and a downregulation of the expression of N-cadherin, Vimentin, and Snail. Conversely, the migration and invasion of Ca Ski TLE4-knockout cells were significantly enhanced, and the expressions of these EMT-related markers showed the opposite trend. Meanwhile, the in vivo xenograft experiment revealed that the Ca Ski TLE4-knockout group exhibited faster tumor growth compared with the wild-type group. Furthermore, we examined the role of TLE4 in the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. In C-33A TLE4-overexpression cells, β-catenin, TCF-1, TCF-4, CyclinD1, c-Myc, and MMP-7 were decreased, p-β-catenin expression was increased, whereas in Ca Ski TLE4-knockout cells, the expression trends of these factors were opposite. After treating TLE4-knockout Ca Ski cells with quercetin, the enhanced migration and invasion capabilities induced by TLE4 knockout were effectively reversed.
CONCLUSION: Quercetin targets and upregulates the expression of TLE4, which inhibits the migration and invasion of cervical cancer cells by blocking the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, thereby providing theoretical and experimental evidence for quercetin therapy in cervical cancer.

abstract: Tropical theileriosis, caused by Theileria annulata, continues to be the most significant tick-borne disease affecting cattle, particularly in endemic regions where it leads to significant production losses. Prompt and reliable diagnosis is critically important for timely treatment and disease control; however, conventional diagnostic methods have important limitations. Microscopic examination lacks sensitivity, particularly in carrier animals, while PCR requires specialized laboratory infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, a fluorescence-based RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay targeting the multicopy mitochondrial cytb gene was developed for rapid detection of T. annulata. Five RPA primer pairs were designed and evaluated, and primer set-5, generating a 324-bp amplicon, exhibited the best amplification performance. A CRISPR RNA (crRNA) was designed within the selected amplicon to enable specific Cas12a-mediated target recognition. The assay was completed within 50 min and demonstrated no cross-reactivity with DNA from Theileria orientalis, Babesia bigemina, Babesia bovis, Anaplasma marginale, and bovine host DNA, confirming excellent analytical specificity. Sensitivity analysis using recombinant plasmid DNA demonstrated a detection limit of approximately ten copies per reaction. The field evaluation of the assay was done by testing 206 bovine field samples. showed that the developed assay identified 163 positive samples, exceeding the detection rates obtained by PCR (151 positives) and microscopy (116 positives). On comparison with PCR, the assay achieved 100% diagnostic sensitivity, 78.18% specificity, 92.64% positive predictive value, 100% negative predictive value, with an overall agreement of 94.17%. These findings indicate that the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a platform is a rapid, sensitive, and accurate molecular diagnostic approach with strong potential for field application and point-of-care diagnosis of bovine tropical theileriosis, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

abstract: Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) prolong survival in prostate cancer, yet durable control is frequently lost through transcriptional adaptation and lineage plasticity. Whether environmental endocrine-disrupting chemicals can actively bias this trajectory and create tractable resistance dependencies remains unclear. Here we show that chronic low-dose exposure to triphenyl phosphate (TPP) induces exposure-conditioned, partially persistent and reversible enzalutamide tolerance in AR-positive prostate cancer cells, accompanied by increased colony formation. Tolerance persists initially after exposure withdrawal but declines during washout, and TPP rechallenge increases GR50 again. A pooled CRISPR screen across two genetic backgrounds converged on MEN1 as the most robust concordant hit, and genetic perturbation and rescue identified a MEN1 dependency that was most apparent in the TPP-conditioned tolerant state. Mechanistically, TPP induced NR1I2 and MEN1 mRNA, endogenous target genes, and PXR-associated reporter activity; antagonist-sensitive transcriptional responses, SPA70-mediated reversal of tolerance, and MEN1-locus regulatory-region visualization were consistent with engagement of a PXR/NR1I2-associated receptor program. Targeted chromatin profiling identified MEN1-dependent changes in H3K4me3, H3K27ac and accessibility at selected AR and plasticity-associated loci. TPP_long reduced H3K4me3 and accessibility at AR loci, while MEN1 CRISPRi opposed the major transcriptional and chromatin changes. In LNCaP-luc xenografts, TPP exposure attenuated enzalutamide-mediated tumor suppression, and MEN1 CRISPRi reduced tumor burden in the TPP + enzalutamide background. This reduction in enzalutamide control was not reproduced in the exploratory VCaP model under androgen deprivation. Together, these data support an exposure-conditioned receptor-to-chromatin model in which MEN1 supports an AR-low/plasticity-high adaptive state.

abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) poses a major public health threat due to high mortality and limited therapeutic options. Rapid and accurate detection of both species identity and resistance determinants is critical for clinical management. Here, we developed a dual-target recombinase polymerase amplification-CRISPR/Cas12a multiplex lateral flow assay (DRC-MLFA) for simultaneous detection of K. pneumoniae and blaKPC in a single reaction. This platform introduces a functionally differentiated dual-channel detection strategy, in which the K. pneumoniae signal is generated directly via RPA-lateral flow readout, while blaKPC detection is achieved through an additional CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated verification step. To enable one-pot integration, suboptimal protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequences were employed to delay Cas12a activation, thereby coordinating amplification and CRISPR detection within a single reaction system. Under optimized conditions, the assay achieved dual-target detection within 50 min at 37 °C, with a limit of detection of 101 CFU/μL and high specificity against non-target pathogens. Validation with 30 clinical samples showed strong concordance with quantitative PCR. This portable and low-cost biosensor provides a practical solution for point-of-care detection of CRKP and establishes a framework for integrating hierarchical specificity control into multiplex CRISPR diagnostics.

abstract: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway is a highly conserved regulator of cellular growth and survival. DEPTOR serves as an endogenous inhibitor of this pathway by directly binding to both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2). While DEPTOR is extensively implicated in oncology and peripheral metabolism, its role in the nervous system remains poorly understood. In this study, we utilized CRISPR/Cas9 technology to disrupt deptor in the zebrafish model to investigate its neurodevelopmental functions. We found that deptor-/- larvae exhibit motor deficits alongside structural axonal abnormalities, characterized by misaligned and broadened axonal tracts. These phenotypes were accompanied by the transcriptional dysregulation of key cholesterol-regulatory genes and progressive, aberrant accumulation of cholesterol from 5 to 10 days post-fertilization. Pharmacological elevation of cholesterol levels recapitulated these axonal and behavioral defects in wild-type larvae, whereas clearance of excess cholesterol successfully rescued the mutant phenotype. Together, our findings demonstrate that deptor deficiency drives cholesterol dysregulation, causing structural and functional abnormalities in the nervous system. This study uncovers a novel link between DEPTOR, lipid homeostasis, and neurodevelopment, highlighting cholesterol metabolism as a potential therapeutic target for neurological disorders associated with mTOR pathway dysfunction.

abstract: Fungal keratitis (FK) remains a major cause of vision-threatening corneal infection, especially in tropical and subtropical regions, with an expanding epidemiological spectrum driven by environmental, climatic, occupational and host-related factors. Fusarium and Aspergillus were the most common pathogens reported. Greater etiological diversity is reflected by increasing recognition of dematiaceous fungi, uncommon molds, and cryptic species. The literature search was performed by searching bibliographic databases (PubMed and Google Scholar), covering publications from January 2000 to August 2026. Additional relevant studies were identified by screening the reference lists of key publications. This review provides an overview of the current state of FK including changing epidemiology, established diagnostic approaches, emerging technologies, and evolving therapeutic approaches. Conventional microscopy and culture remain central to diagnosis, with molecular methods, sequencing, MALDI-TOF and noninvasive imaging offering advantages in sensitivity, speed and species-level identification. Novel diagnostic methods such as CRISPR-based tests, genome sequencing, artificial intelligence, biosensors and point-of-care diagnostics may provide rapid and accessible precision diagnosis. Therapeutic challenges include poor corneal drug penetration, antifungal resistance and prolonged treatment. Hence, the exploration of new antifungals, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, photoactivated therapies and antimicrobial peptides. These advances support a transition to integrated, rapid and precision-based management of FK collectively.

abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype characterized by the absence of targetable receptors and limited therapeutic options. Its inherently low immunogenicity necessitates strategies to enhance its susceptibility to immune attack. This study aimed to enhance the antitumor immune response by inducing downregulation of the programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), thereby increasing cancer cell recognition and activating tumor-specific immunity. To this end, a targeted solid lipid nanoparticle (tSLN) system was developed for the precise delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids to achieve functional PD-L1 downregulation. The SLN formulation comprised a cetyl palmitate core stabilized with cationic and PEGylated lipids. Functionalization with the tumor-penetrating peptide iRGD yielded tSLN, which demonstrated good colloidal stability, serum protection of the CRISPR cargo, and minimal cytotoxicity. In vitro studies in two breast cancer subtypes, the luminal MCF-7 and the triple-negative 4T1 line, confirmed greater transfection efficiency and PD-L1 knockdown by tSLN:Crispr/PD-L1 relative to non-targeted controls. In an orthotopic 4T1 mouse model, systemic administration of tSLN:Crispr/PD-L1 significantly inhibited tumor growth and metastasis while enhancing T cell infiltration, and was more effective than standard chemotherapy (paclitaxel) in this model. The targeted approach also exhibited a favorable short-term safety profile, with no organ toxicity detected over the treatment period. These findings underscore the potential of SLN-mediated CRISPR delivery as an immunomodulatory strategy for breast cancer, and particularly for TNBC.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, encoding an elongated polyglutamine stretch in the corresponding mutant HTT (mHTT) protein. HD pathogenesis is driven by multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species, including HTT1a and repeat-associated non-AUG translation (RAN) proteins, which increase in expression as mutant CAG repeats lengthen due to somatic expansion. VO659 is an investigational CAG repeat-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that lowers mHTT protein levels by blocking translation. Here, we show that VO659 allele-preferentially lowers levels of multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species in a CAG repeat length-dependent manner, relatively sparing wild-type HTT, while becoming more efficacious as somatic expansion occurs. VO659 reduced HTT1a mRNA levels in HD fibroblasts with an ultra-long CAG repeat, blocked the translation of HTT1a and polyalanine-containing RAN proteins derived from HTT exon 1 overexpression constructs, and displayed a long tissue half-life in mouse brain, supporting an infrequent dosing regimen. A first-in-human, open-label phase 1/2a clinical trial (NCT05822908) is currently ongoing in HD patients. VO659's unique CAG repeat-dependent and allele-preferential mechanism of action holds promise for its therapeutic effect in HD patients by targeting multiple core neurotoxic proteins derived from (somatically) expanded mHTT CAG repeats, while sparing wild-type HTT expression.

abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent disorder characterized by excessive hepatic lipid accumulation, frequently progressing to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Transcription factor EB (TFEB) coordinates lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy, and lipid catabolism, and therefore represents a potential therapeutic target; however, safe and direct strategies for selectively enhancing hepatic TFEB activity remain limited. Here, liver-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) were developed to deliver mRNAs encoding wild-type TFEB or the constitutively active TFEB S211A mutant, and their efficacy was evaluated in cellular and choline-deficient, L-amino acid-defined high-fat diet (CDAHFD)-induced mouse models of MASLD. LNP-mediated delivery increased hepatic TFEB expression, enhanced autophagic flux, and reprogrammed metabolic pathways toward fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A and ACOX1) while suppressing the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g., FASN, ACC, and SREBP1). Consequently, targeted TFEB mRNA therapy significantly reduced hepatic triglyceride content, attenuated steatosis, lowered MASLD activity scores, and decreased fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling, ChIP-qPCR, promoter-reporter assays, and targeted knockdown models indicated that TFEB exerts its protective effects against lipid accumulation at least partly by transcriptionally activating the fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings establish LNP-mediated TFEB mRNA delivery as a useful preclinical approach for investigating hepatic biology and provide a targeted, transient, and non-integrating genetic strategy with potential for the treatment of MASLD.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated transcription factor EB mRNA delivery for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted global supply chains, causing shortages of critical lipid-based raw materials for mRNA vaccine production. To enhance formulation resilience, we systematically evaluated the impact of five ionizable lipids (ILs) on lipid nanoparticle (LNP) organization, mRNA delivery and immunogenicity. The physiochemical analysis revealed the potential coexistence of liquid crystalline lamellar (Lα) and inverse hexagonal (HII) phases, or a mixture of nucleotide-loaded and non-loaded HII phases within developed LNP formulations. Furthermore, ILs with saturated, multi-tail structures, such as Lipid-5 and SM-102, favored inverse hexagonal (HII) internal organization and fusion intermediates, correlating with enhanced endosomal fusion and higher in vivo protein expression. In contrast, ILs such as cKK-E12, which featured dual ionization headgroups and tended to form lamellar-like structures, showed reduced encapsulation efficiency and transfection potency. The preclinical experiments demonstrated that all developed formulations induced robust binding and neutralizing antibody responses; however, antibody responses were lower in mRNA Lipid 5 LNPs and mRNA SM-102 LNPs than in other formulations. Notably, within the limited panel of ILs in this study, protein expression levels did not show a clear correlation with antibody titers, highlighting that efficient antigen expression alone is not predictive of humoral immunity. These findings underscore how IL structural features influence LNP architecture and function, informing the rational design of next-generation mRNA vaccines.

title: Ionizable lipid impact on mRNA vaccine formulation properties and immunogenicity.

abstract: Chemical modifications of RNA bases and adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing are regulatory layers essentially unexplored in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), whose oxidative dysfunction underlies age-related macular degeneration. We mapped both layers in ARPE-19 cells exposed to tert-butyl hydroperoxide under two non-pharmacological interventions, Quantum Molecular Resonance (QMR) electrotherapy and a patient blood-derived secretome, across 56 libraries spanning four arms, three time points and matched stressed and stress-free conditions (GEO: GSE328981). Base modifications were called with HARMLNC and A-to-I editing screened with a transition-signal caller, then re-analysed with REDItools3, JACUSA2 and LoDEI. The high-confidence set comprised 241 calls at 15 sites, all of classes canonical to tRNA and rRNA. The most prevalent was an adenosine modification at chrM:2617 in mitochondrial 16S rRNA (MT-RNR2), detected in 51 of 56 libraries and in every arm. Two positions 1 bp apart lie in an EZR/SYTL3 overlap region, whereas a third chromosome 6 site maps to HLA-C, 127.5 Mb away. No position of either layer differed between treatment arms: 7 testable modification sites (minimum p = 0.19) and, at single-nucleotide resolution under dedicated callers agreeing to r = 0.975-0.992, 15 curated editing positions (minimum q = 0.169). Two one-sided tests bound any change in substitution composition within 1.4% and in mean editing frequency within 10% for secretome and combination and 20% for QMR. Against a stress-free baseline internal to the cohort, only chrM:13710 (MT-ND5) changed detectably (q = 0.03). These layers are therefore small, largely constitutive and quantifiably undisturbed by either intervention at the resolution available.

title: RNA base-modification and A-to-I editing landscapes of oxidatively stressed human retinal pigment epithelium under Quantum Molecular Resonance electrotherapy and blood-derived secretome.

abstract: Advanced heart failure affects over 6 million adults in the United States alone. Orthotopic heart transplantation remains the definitive treatment, with over 90% one-year survival and meaningful gains in functional status and quality of life. The therapy is, however, constrained by an intractable supply problem. For decades, xenotransplantation (XTx), the transplantation of organs across species, has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, though for most of that time it remained a theoretical aspiration. With the discovery of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, improved immunosuppressive strategies, and refined preclinical models, the field has accelerated at an unprecedented pace. Multi-gene-edited porcine donors have survived for more than 200 days in orthotopic non-human primate models, and two compassionate-use pig-to-human cardiac transplants at the University of Maryland (2022 and 2023) demonstrated some feasibility for clinical cardiac XTx for the first time. In May 2026, the FDA granted clearance under an investigational new drug application to allow the EXPRESS study, the first prospective clinical trial of a gene-edited porcine heart, to proceed. In this perspective, we discuss the ethical, regulatory, and equity considerations that remain as decisive barriers to clinical integration and may shape how this therapy is introduced along the remaining immunologic and virologic challenges. We outline what we regard as the near-term priorities: defining the antibody targets that drive xenograft rejection, standardizing virologic surveillance, candidate selection and outcome benchmarking, and building access patterns with embedded distributive justice from the outset of its implementation.

title: Advancing cardiac xenotransplantation: overcoming challenges and ethical considerations for clinical integration.

abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of death worldwide, yet therapeutic development is limited by experimental models that incompletely recapitulate human physiology, disease heterogeneity, and treatment responses. Emerging human-relevant models, including patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells, cardiac organoids, engineered tissues, organ-on-chip systems, genome editing, multi-omics, and computational approaches, are improving the ability to investigate cardiovascular disease mechanisms and therapeutic responses. In this review, we critically compare these technologies with respect to physiological relevance, reproducibility, scalability, throughput, and translational potential. We highlight their applications in disease modeling, drug discovery, toxicity assessment, and precision medicine while examining persistent limitations, including cellular immaturity, incomplete vascularization and systemic integration, model variability, and limited clinical validation. We further discuss how integration of bioengineering, genome editing, multi-omics, and computational methods may improve predictive performance. Standardization, interlaboratory validation, regulatory qualification, and prospective benchmarking against human clinical outcomes will be essential for translating these platforms into reliable tools for cardiovascular research and therapeutic development. Collectively, the convergence of stem cell biology, bioengineering, genome editing, multi-omics, and computational approaches is establishing a new generation of human-centered cardiovascular models with the potential to strengthen mechanistic discovery and accelerate the development of more predictive and personalized therapies.

abstract: Large insert gene editing in ex vivo, primary human T cells represents an important approach for engineering next-generation cellular immunotherapies. While CRISPR-based editing is well-established for small genetic modifications, large insert knock-in remains a technical bottleneck. This review examines current strategies for achieving efficient, precise and safe integration of large genetic elements. We compare delivery methods for CRISPR components, highlighting electroporation of Cas9 ribonucleoproteins as the most efficient but often cytotoxic approach; emerging alternatives such as cell-penetrating peptides and lipid nanoparticles offer improved cell viability at the expense of editing efficiency. The influence of genomic locus selection, guide RNA design and chromatin context on editing outcomes, as well as the role of homology-directed repair (HDR) template design is evaluated. Various template formats-including linear double- and single-stranded DNA, plasmids, circular single-stranded (css) DNA and recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV)-are assessed for their efficiency, toxicity and risk of off-target integration. Where possible, cross-study normalisation is used to enable meaningful comparisons. rAAV templates consistently achieve the highest insertion rates but come with concerns regarding cost, size limitations and insertional mutagenesis, whereas non-viral approaches such as cssDNA templates show promise. Additionally, we review the use of small-molecule modulators to enhance HDR efficiency, noting trade-offs between improved insertion rates and potential genomic instability. Overall, successful large insert editing requires balancing of editing efficiency, cell viability and genomic safety considerations. Continued optimisation of delivery systems, template design and repair pathway modulation will be critical for advancing scalable and clinically viable T-cell therapies.

title: From delivery to integration: CRISPR-mediated large insert gene editing in primary human T cells.

abstract: This protocol describes a method for endogenous protein tagging in postmitotic primary neurons using homology-independent targeted integration (HITI), a CRISPR/Cas9-based approach that exploits non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Unlike homology-directed repair (HDR), HITI does not require cell division, making it uniquely suited for postmitotic neurons. SpCas9 is delivered by a replication-incompetent simian immunodeficiency lentiviral vector (pLenti SIV), while the sgRNA, donor tag cassette, and a fluorescent plasma membrane marker are co-packaged in a single AAV vector. The two vectors are co-delivered at DIV5, and endogenous tagging is assessed at DIV15-23. The workflow is illustrated using Junctophilin-3 (JPH3) tagged with mEmerald at its endogenous locus. Airyscan microscopy imaging of endogenously tagged JPH3 at native expression levels revealed its localization at endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane (ER-PM) contact sites and uncovered a periodic distribution of ER-PM junctions along the dendritic arbor, enabling identification of a previously unrecognized ladder-like organization of the ER in neuronal dendrites. Genomic integration of the tag is validated at both 5' and 3' junctions by next-generation sequencing. The protocol can be adapted to other neuronal proteins by redesigning the guide RNA and donor sequence, and supports fluorescent proteins as well as epitope and self-labeling tags. The plasma membrane marker can also be replaced with other fluorescent reporters or markers for intracellular organelles to assess infection efficiency and verify subcellular localization of the protein of interest. The full workflow takes 5-6 weeks. © 2026 The Author(s). Current Protocols published by Wiley Periodicals LLC. Protocols included in this article: Basic Protocol 1: sgRNA design and HITI donor vector cloning Basic Protocol 2: Primary rat neuron culture and viral co-transduction Basic Protocol 3: Live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged proteins Support Protocol 1: Production of lentiviral and AAV particles Support Protocol 2: Validation of knock-in by next-generation sequencing (NGS).

abstract: Bacterial infection is a major cause of delayed wound healing, while overuse of antibiotics has accelerated the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Developing multifunctional antibacterial biomaterials that eradicate bacteria without relying on conventional antibiotics is therefore highly desirable. Herein, we report an injectable polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based hydrogel incorporating gold nanorods (ARs) and a DNA nanostructure-mediated silver and antisense oligonucleotide delivery system (A-C@Ag) to achieve synergistic antibacterial therapy and enhanced skin regeneration. The hydrogel is formed by rapid thiol-maleimide crosslinking of PEG precursors containing AR@A-C@Ag, providing excellent injectability, biocompatibility, and mechanical stability. Upon near-infrared irradiation, the AR generates mild photothermal heating to directly damage bacteria and simultaneously promotes the on-demand release of Ag+ and antisense oligonucleotides from the DNA nanostructure, resulting in markedly enhanced antibacterial activity against both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli by facilitating bacterial membrane disruption. In a S. aureus-infected full-thickness wound model, AR@A-C@Ag/Gel under NIR irradiation significantly accelerated wound closure by efficiently eliminating bacteria, suppressing inflammation, promoting angiogenesis and collagen deposition, and facilitating the regeneration of skin appendages. This work demonstrates that integrating DNA nanostructure-enabled drug delivery with mild photothermal therapy represents an effective strategy for constructing antibiotic-free antibacterial hydrogels for infected wound repair.

abstract: Background: Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) in smooth muscle cells (SMCs) is essential for maintaining aortic wall integrity. This study investigated whether deletion of LRP1 in SMCs induces region-specific aortic pathology and evaluated a potential therapeutic strategy. Methods: Lrp1-floxed mice were bred with Sm22-Cre+/0 mice to generate mice with SMC-LRP1 deletion (SMC-LRP1-/-) and wild-type littermates (SMC-LRP1+/+). Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) was used to visualize the aorta, and aortic tissue sections were characterized histologically. To evaluate a potential therapeutic strategy, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting hepatocyte-derived angiotensinogen (AGT) were administered to inhibit AGT synthesis. Results: Immunostaining and Western blotting confirmed LRP1 deletion in aortic SMCs. At 40 weeks of age, micro-CT revealed marked increases in aortic width and volume. Although dilatation occurred throughout the aorta, the infrarenal region exhibited the greatest expansion in both male and female SMC-LRP1-/- mice compared with SMC-LRP1+/+ littermates; subsequent analyses therefore focused on this region. LRP1 deletion in SMCs caused pronounced SMC loss and increased collagen deposition in the infrarenal aorta. Inhibition of hepatocyte-derived AGT with ASO attenuated infrarenal aortic dilatation and preserved aortic wall integrity in both male and female mice. Conclusions: Deletion of LRP1 in SMCs causes progressive aortic dilatation that includes the infrarenal aorta. Pharmacologic inhibition of hepatocyte-derived AGT attenuates infrarenal aortic dilatation.

abstract: Most RNA-cleaving DNAzymes are limited to cleaving between combinations of the four canonical ribonucleotides. Through in vitro selection, we isolated ICD11-1T, a DNAzyme that selectively cleaves at inosine, a non-canonical RNA modification generated by adenosine deamination. ICD11-1T cleaves inosine-containing substrates with a rate constant of 0.1 min-1 and achieves >103-fold selectivity over adenosine, discriminating between nucleosides that differ at the C6 and N1 positions of the purine ring. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the inosine positions the cleavage site near the catalytic core, whereas the adenosine complex sequesters it away, accounting for the stringent specificity. Using ICD11-1T, we constructed a fluorescent biosensor that enabled imaging of endogenous ADAR (adenosine deaminase acting on RNA) editing activity in fixed and permeabilized cells. This work provides a proof-of-concept tool for studying adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing and establishes a strategy for expanding the functionality of DNAzymes.

title: Exploiting inosine as a distinctive cleavage site for deriving a highly specific RNA-cleaving DNAzyme.

abstract: Conventional and transgenic approaches to crop improvement are increasingly constrained by biosafety concerns, stringent regulatory frameworks, and limited public acceptance, necessitating new precision breeding methods. DNA-free genome editing using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach has emerged as a transformative approach that enables precise, targeted genetic modifications without the stable integration of a foreign gene (transgene). This strategy transiently introduces CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, or in vitro transcribed mRNA, into plant cells. This review focuses primarily on CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing and its applications in crop improvement. After targeted genome cleavage, the editing elements are rapidly degraded, leaving only the desired genomic modification and resulting in plants indistinguishable from those developed through conventional breeding. To achieve targeted, DNA-free genome editing, researchers have developed numerous molecular platforms and delivery systems, such as protoplast transfection, biolistic bombardment, nanoparticle-based systems, and emerging pollen- and meristem-targeted systems, for major crop species. Researchers have successfully enhanced several notable traits, including disease and pest resistance, nutritional quality, abiotic stress tolerance, and agronomic performance, in cereals, vegetables, oilseeds, and perennial crops. Recent advancements, including base editing, prime editing, and multiplex gene editing, are further expanding the precision, efficiency, and scope of DNA-free genome editing. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing offers a route to crop improvement that avoids stable transgene integration, though its wider deployment depends on progress in regeneration, molecular validation, and regulatory convergence.

title: Genome editing beyond transgenes: DNA-free technologies in crop improvement.

abstract: Preeclampsia originates in placental dysfunction yet it is detected only after maternal hypertension and proteinuria or other organ damage emerge, by which point disease-modifying interventions are not available, and delivery of the baby and placenta remains the only cure. Nanotechnology offers a route to reduce this diagnostic-therapeutic latency. Nanostructured biosensors and liquid biopsy platforms detect placental proteins, cell-free RNA/DNA, and extracellular vesicles at femtomolar concentrations and in a multiplex manner, enabling earlier risk stratification when integrated with machine-learning models. In parallel, placenta-targeted lipid-, peptide-, polymeric-, dendrimeric-, and small extracellular vesicle-based nanocarriers deliver angiogenic mRNA, antiangiogenic siRNA, antioxidants, and immunomodulators selectively to the trophoblast cells while limiting fetal exposure. Placenta-on-a-chip platforms and ex vivo placental perfusion models provide human-relevant test beds for these systems. We critically appraise these advances, examine the safety-by-design, manufacturing bottlenecks, and regulatory constraints unique to obstetric nanomedicine, and outline the convergence of theranostics and digital health that could move preeclampsia care from reactive symptom management toward proactive, placenta-targeted monitoring and therapy.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 relies on a dual CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) guide, yet whether RNA-based anti-CRISPRs exist for this system has remained unknown. Here, we identify a phage-encoded small non-coding RNA, rAcrIIA1, that adopts an unexpected chimeric crRNA-tracrRNA architecture, faithfully recapitulating the entire single-guide RNA (sgRNA) of Cas9. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Cas9-rAcrIIA1 binary complex and the Cas9-rAcrIIA1-DNA ternary complex reveal that rAcrIIA1 engages Cas9 nearly identically to the native sgRNA, competitively blocking crRNA and tracrRNA loading and thereby abolishing DNA interference. Strikingly, beyond its natural inhibitory function, rAcrIIA1 is fully reprogrammable: with variable guide sequences, it directs Cas9 for sequence-specific DNA cleavage with efficiency comparable to the canonical sgRNA, and it activates trans-cleavage more potently. Thus, rAcrIIA1 provides an experimentally validated, mechanistically resolved RNA-based inhibitor of CRISPR-Cas9, reveals a distinct anti-CRISPR mechanism through complete sgRNA mimicry, and serves as a versatile bifunctional scaffold for genome editing and diagnostics.

abstract: Understanding how an RNA recognizes small molecule ligands is crucial for pharmaceutical research. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can potentially reveal this process in atomistic detail. However, simulations frequently fail should energy barriers along the pathway prove to be insurmountably high on the simulation timescale (ns-µs). To address this limitation, we present a novel strategy combining well-tempered metadynamics utilizing X-ray crystallography or NMR-solved hydrogen-bonding interactions between an RNA and its ligand as collective variables (CVs). This approach can sample multiple transitions during the binding process and determine the most favorable binding modes through the reconstructed free energy landscape. Our computational recovery of binding modes for all five cases studied is in good agreement (RMSD below 2.0 Å) with the experimentally determined structures of the bound complexes. Our study demonstrates that metadynamics coupled with strategically chosen collective variables can effectively sample binding pathways and recover binding modes for RNA-small molecule complexes. This method therefore could be valuable for crystal structure interpretation, NMR solution structure refinement, and computer-aided design of RNA-targeted small molecule drugs.

abstract: The major goal of this study is to evaluate a new type of cell transplantation therapy for individuals with hereditary PAP, study a new treatment that may be useful for treatment of other diseases, and research mechanisms that drive the development and function of lung macrophages.

description:
Hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (hPAP) is a rare lung disease characterized by the progressive accumulation of pulmonary surfactant in alveoli resulting in progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure, and in some patients, secondary infections and/or pulmonary fibrosis. While hPAP affects men, women, and children, most patients present as children. The lung structure appears well-preserved in many cases with pathogenesis being driven by the consequences of the filling of alveoli with surfactant sediment; however, some patients develop respiratory failure caused by pulmonary fibrosis requiring therapeutic lung transplantation.

Hereditary PAP is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the genes (CSF2RA or CSF2RB) encoding the GM-CSF receptor alpha or beta chains, respectively. Mutations in these genes disrupt GM-CSF receptor function, blocking GM-CSF signaling and impairing the removal of excess surfactant from alveoli by alveolar macrophages (AMs).

This study is an open-label, non-randomized, single center clinical treatment study to evaluate the feasibility of manufacturing CSF2RA gene-corrected macrophages, as well as the safety, tolerability, efficacy, and durability of CSF2RA gene correction/pulmonary macrophage transplantation (PMT) therapy in three patients with hPAP caused by recessive homozygous or compound heterozygous CSF2RA mutations. In addition to safety and tolerability, the clinical trial will evaluate outcome measures related to clinical efficacy and biologic signature of CSF2RA gene-correction/PMT therapy, as well as pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and the mechanism of action.

The clinical trial design includes a 2-month observation period, a Baseline visit, 5-month treatment period, and Short-, Medium-, and Long-Term follow-up periods of 1, 4, and 10 years, respectively. Each patient will serve as their own self-control and receive a split-dose comprising three administrations of autologous, bone marrow cluster of differentiation 34+ (CD34+) cell-derived, lentiviral CSF2RA gene-corrected macrophages at a minimum of 2-month intervals, delivered by direct bronchoscopic instillation of cells into individual lung segments (5.8x105 cells/segment); an increasing number of cells at each administration will be achieved by sequentially increasing the number of segments treated. Current standard medical care (whole lung lavage and supplemental oxygen) will be continuously available to all enrolled patients.

Assessments will include safety (adverse events and serious adverse events), tolerability (short-term, treatment-emergent pulmonary symptoms), efficacy (beneficial effects on clinical, physiological, and radiological manifestations of hPAP), durability (persistence of beneficial effects), and mechanism of action (persistence, CSF2RA-expression, and function of alveolar macrophages (AMs)).

Expected results will inform the feasibility, safety, tolerability, efficacy, durability, and mechanism of action of gene transfer/PMT as therapy of hPAP. These results will impact the field because it departs markedly from the current inefficient, highly invasive method of physically removing surfactant by whole lung lavage (WLL) and instead uses a novel approach to restore AM function. This study is expected to establish the feasibility of a novel, specific therapy for children with hPAP and a new type of cell transplantation therapy (PMT) that may be useful for other diseases.

The current severity of hPAP (PGIS) will be assessed on a five-point scale ranging from none, mild, moderate, severe, to very severe.

The change from baseline in hPAP severity (PGIC) will be assessed on a five-point scale ranging from much improved, somewhat improved, no change, somewhat worse, to much worse.

The PGIS and PGIC parameters will be evaluated just prior to PMT, immediately upon completion of PMT, and daily for 5 days following PMT.

description:
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of all diagnoses. For patients with metastatic NSCLC lacking actionable driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, ALK), the standard first-line therapeutic strategy involves immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) or programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) axis, administered either as monotherapy or in combination with platinum-doublet chemotherapy. While these regimens have significantly improved overall survival (OS), a substantial proportion of patients fail to derive durable clinical benefit, and long-term survival rates for metastatic disease remain suboptimal, often due to host-related factors that impair the anti-tumor immune response.

A critical determinant of poor therapeutic outcomes in advanced NSCLC is cancer-associated cachexia (CAC), a multifactorial paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by systemic inflammation, negative protein-energy balance, and the involuntary loss of skeletal muscle mass (sarcopenia). Primary observational studies demonstrate that nutritional derangements closely associated with cachexia - such as significant weight loss and malnutrition - are highly prevalent in lung cancer, particularly in advanced disease, with lung cancer-specific cohorts reporting rates ranging from approximately 35% - 70% depending on disease stage and assessment method. Unlike starvation, it is driven by aberrant systemic inflammation and not fully reversible via nutritional support.

Clinically, cachexia is defined by the international consensus (Fearon criteria) as weight loss \>5% over 6 months, or weight loss \>2% in individuals with a body mass index (BMI) \< 20 kg/m2 or sarcopenia. Sarcopenia is specifically defined by a low skeletal muscle index (SMI) at the L3 vertebral level, with widely validated cutoffs of \< 52.4 cm2/m2 for men and \< 8.5 cm2/m2 for women.

This is a Phase 1b/2, multi-site, single-arm, open-label, non-randomized study looking at whether adding tocilizumab to standard treatment for metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) is safe, possible, and effective. The study includes people with metastatic NSCLC, that is lung cancer that has spread, who have experienced significant loss of weight or muscle mass.

Primary Objective Evaluate the safety/feasibility and efficacy of adding tocilizumab to standard first-line chemo-immunotherapy in biomarker-selected patients with stage IV NSCLC, defined by weight loss ≥5% within the prior 6 months, or ≥2% if BMI \< 20 kg/m².

Co-primary endpoint 1: Safety/Feasibility Proportion of patients completing four cycles of chemo-IO + tocilizumab without grade ≥3 autoimmune or non-hematological treatment-related adverse events (TRAE). Feasibility will be defined as ≥80% completion; unacceptable toxicity as \>30% incidence of grade ≥3 serious AEs.

Co-primary endpoint 2: Progression-Free Survival Rate at 6 months Proportion of patients alive and progression-free at 6 months after starting therapy per RECIST v1.1, estimated by Kaplan-Meier and presented with a 95% CI.

Secondary Objectives Assess the effect of tocilizumab on body composition, inflammatory biomarkers, and treatment response.

Secondary Endpoints: change in weight/muscle mass (CT-based sarcopenia/Fearon index); Overall Response Rate (ORR); median Overall Survival Rate; and CRP levels from baseline to end of treatment.

Correlative Objectives Evaluate associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and baseline inflammatory biomarkers (CRP) as well as molecular biomarkers (KRAS, STK11) identified by next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumor tissue.

Exploratory Objectives Identify associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and longitudinal measurements of CRP, IL-6, Cyclin D1 and Bcl-xL mRNA, as well as baseline PTPRT methylation.

Participants will go through the screening and baseline process to assess eligibility. If eligible, participants will attend study treatment visits every 21 days for about 3 months, an End of Treatment (EOT) visit about 30 days after the last dose of treatment, and follow up for up to 12 months after the EOT visit. Tocilizumab will be administered in addition to standard treatment regimens for NSCLC, at a dose of 8 mg/kg intravenous (IV) once every three weeks (once every 21 days); on day one of each treatment cycle. Tocilizumab is administered as a single IV drip infusion over 1 hour; it cannot be administered as bolus or push. Tocilizumab will be given for 4 doses, at the beginning of treatment, or until disease progression or unacceptable toxicities.

The study will be open at 4 VA hospitals, and planned enrollment is about 43 participants in total with about 11 participants from each site. This research study is expected to take about 4 years. Individual participation in the study will take about 18 months.

abstract: In June 2026, satri-cel/CT041, a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell product targeting Claudin18.2, received approval from China's National Medical Products Administration for the treatment of Claudin18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma after failure of at least two prior lines of therapy. This marks the first CAR-T product approved worldwide for solid tumours. The approval ends the long-standing debate over whether CAR-T cells can be effective against solid malignancies, yet it simultaneously raises a more pointed issue: in its pivotal randomised controlled trial, median progression-free survival was 3.25 months (95% CI 2.86-4.53) with satri-cel against 1.77 months (95% CI 1.61-2.04) with treatment of physician's choice, giving a hazard ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.24-0.56). The two medians differ by 1.48 months; that figure marks where each survival distribution is cut in half and is not the benefit any individual patient can expect, and approval does not equate to a cure. Taking this as a starting point, this review systematically dissects the immunological bottlenecks that constrain CAR-T efficacy in gastrointestinal tumours. We first trace the evidence chain from phase I studies through the randomised controlled trial to exploratory adjuvant-therapy settings and then integrate the landscape of targets-Claudin18.2, glypican-3, carcinoembryonic antigen, mesothelin, and CDH17-within a target-tumour matrix encompassing gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic cancer. The core section focuses on four intertwined immunological constraints: spatiotemporal heterogeneity and escape at the antigen level; a therapeutic window shaped jointly by epitope masking within tight junctions and immune privilege of the gastric mucosal stem cell niche-this mechanism not only explains why Claudin18.2-directed CAR-T cells exhibit an acceptable safety profile despite target expression on normal tissues but also provides a paradigm for rational selection of next-generation targets; a suppressive microenvironment composed of regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, tumour-associated macrophages, transforming growth factor-β, adenosine, and a hypoxic and acidotic metabolic milieu; and CAR-T exhaustion driven by chronic antigen stimulation. We particularly emphasise that metabolic stress and exhaustion are not two parallel obstacles. We put forward a mechanistic model in which persistent antigen stimulation combined with intratumoral hypoxia acts as a "double hit": through mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species accumulation, the two inputs raise nuclear factor of activated T-cell (NFAT) activity and so drive the TOX/NR4A-dominated exhaustion program. This model is assembled from chronic-infection and mouse tumour systems and has not been tested in human CAR-T cells or in satri-cel-treated patients. We advance it as a framework for organising the four bottlenecks and for explaining why single-point interventions struggle to lift the efficacy ceiling, not as a demonstrated account. On this basis, we discuss strategies such as armouring, logic gating, transcription factor engineering, gene editing, and chemokine receptor modification, along with combination regimens involving checkpoint inhibition, oncolytic viruses, locoregional administration, and microbiome modulation, and we evaluate alternative platforms including CAR-macrophages, CAR-NK cells, and in vivo CAR-T generation. The watershed has been crossed, but the work of turning 3 months into 30 has only just begun.

abstract:
This exploratory trial will have three parts. Part A is a dose escalation part, Part B is an expanded safety and dose evaluation part, and Part C is a safety and immunogenicity evaluation part in individuals with recurrent HSV-2 genital herpes.

Part A will focus on the safety evaluations, and in addition, vaccine-induced immune responses (specifically neutralizing antibodies) will also be analyzed to assess if there is a dose-response.

Part B of the trial will expand the safety characterization for two dose levels of BNT163 selected based on Part A data and will also enable a more comprehensive assessment of the impact of pre-existing immunity to HSV-1 and -2 on the safety and immune responses to BNT163.

Part C will evaluate safety and immunogenicity of BNT163 compared to a placebo in a three-dose regimen in participants with a history of HSV-2 recurrent genital herpes.
description:
In Part A, participants will be randomized 5:1 to BNT163:placebo. In Part B, participants will be randomized 1:1 to either of the two selected dose levels based on data from Part A. In Part C, participants will be randomized 1:1 to BNT163:placebo.

In Part A \& B, participants will receive three intramuscular doses of a fixed dose level of the BNT163 vaccine (Part A and B) or placebo (Part A only).

In Part C, participants will receive three intramuscular doses of one fixed dose level of the BNT163 vaccine or placebo. In this part, continuous suppressive antiviral therapy is given over the entire vaccine dosing period (during and between vaccine doses) to prevent administration of the vaccine concomitantly to viral replication and active genital herpes.

abstract: We aimed to study the stability of a Beta (β)-SARS-CoV-2 virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine in a series of preliminary experiments using selective stabilizing excipients. β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were produced and purified using established methodologies. The thermostability of VLPs was tested at 4°C and -30°C in the presence or absence of stabilizers polysorbate 80, sorbitol, or L-histidine in the presence of a physiological NaCl concentration of 137 mM. The integrity of VLPs was assessed using ELISA, Western immunoblot, and dynamic light scatter (DLS). β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were stable at 4°C for 14 days, and the addition of stabilizing excipients improved stability compared to VLPs in PBS alone. Storage of VLPs at -80°C maintained particle integrity by DLS analysis for up to 2 years. Excipients helped to maintain the antigenicity of the VLPs by ELISA and Western immunoblot, and DLS analysis revealed that VLPs retained their particulate structure.IMPORTANCESARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally and cause significant illness. The problem of waning immunity to mRNA/LNPs has necessitated frequent boosters to keep pace with emerging variants. The development of alternative vaccines, therefore, remains a priority. Protein- based vaccines, like VLPs, offer a safe alternative able to produce longer-lasting immune responses. In this preliminary stability analysis, the β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were found to be stable at 4°C, and the addition of excipients improved VLP stability. Storage of VLPs at -30°C and -80°C also showed that the VLPs are stable for extended periods. Our findings will be of importance for the ongoing development of a SARS-CoV-2 VLP-based vaccine.
